name: Bera
world_status: a description exists but is not accessible
sweep_summary: Bera (bera1259, Plains Bira, Bantu D32) is not in the catalog and the sweep found no word-stress statement. The single title hit, Maeyens 1938 'Het inlandsch lied en het muzikaal accent met semantische functie bij de Babira' (Kongo-Overzee 4(5):250-259), is about lexical tone ('woordmelodie', 'muzikaal accent') and how Bira song melodies track it, as shown by Google Books search-only snippets of the 1938 volume (id drkWAQAAMAAJ, view_no_pages) and by Brandel 1961's summary (kókó 'chicken' high-level, kapè 'visible' falling, hîga 'hearth' two falling tones on the first syllable). Feed searches for stress vocabulary (klemtoon, dynamisch accent, nadruk, sterkte, expiratorisch) with Babira give no hit in that volume. The article's text could not be obtained (print; archive.org has Kongo-Overzee only for 1950-56; HathiTrust and Google Books page views blocked from our machine; Relevance: prosody-but-not-word-stress; acquisition priority low. Evidence (gbooks_feeds/*.xml) and logged in there. The earlier general audit of this language (same folder) already found that no accessible source (Meinhof 1938-39, Kutsch Lojenga 2003, Gregoire 2003) states where stress falls in Bira; Gregoire 2003:357 reports three level tones.

earlier_scan.note: Glottolog lists only Kutsch Lojenga 2003 subclassification comments; no grammar/phonology found.

sources.note: Bibliographic only. Identifies the descriptive works: Meinhof 1938-39 ZES 29:241-287 (grammar sketch; WALS source for 'bia'); Susa Dz'ba Dheli 1972 (iv+170 pp) and 1974 (iii+76 pp) grammar sketches; Manesane Bogyonokoli 2012 ISP-Bunia phonology memoire; Maeyens 1938 Kongo-Overzee 4(5):250-259 on 'muzikaal accent met semantische functie' (tone); Rzewuski 1988; Vorbichler 1968; de Wit 1995 SIL survey; Rietkerk 1990. WALS (on file) has no stress-feature values (13A-17A) for 'bia'.

sources.citation: Gregoire, Claire. 2003. The Bantu languages of the forest. In D. Nurse & G. Philippson (eds.), The Bantu Languages, 349-370. London: Routledge. (same on-disk text layer; pp.353, 355, 357 excerpted)
sources.note: No stress statement. p.357: 'some northernmost languages of zone D and C have three tones: high, mid and low. This is the case in Bira (D21) [sic - D21 is Bali; Bira is D32 elsewhere in the chapter] and in Nyali (D33)... However, the tone systems of these languages are not sufficiently known yet.' Second-hand, and the D21/D32 slip makes the attribution to Bera uncertain.

sources.citation: Kutsch Lojenga, Constance. 2003. Bila (D32). In D. Nurse & G. Philippson (eds.), The Bantu Languages, 450-474. London: Routledge. (publisher companion-site text layer, Part 2, already on file; pp.450-452 + bibliography excerpted)
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: online with a university library login (also: harvard online access (harvardkey))
sources.note: Nothing on Bira (Plains Bira) prosody. pp.450-452 only establish that Bira [Gera] 'Plains Bira' (D32) and Bila [Gila] 'Forest Bira' are separate languages (~59-60% cognates) and group Bira with Amba, Bhele, Bila, Kaiku, Kango, Komo (7 vowels, collapsed noun classes); the phonology and tone sections (three level tones + downstep) describe Bila only; no stress/accent statement anywhere in the chapter.
Stub (D32, 120,000 speakers 1992, 'close to Amba'); no phonology, tone or stress information.

sources.quote: Kongo-Overzee 1938 snippets: "... woord met gelijkmatige hooge of lage woordmelodie behoudt deze eigenschap in ... toon van de eerste stamklankgreep. Zie lied 5: hîgă (haard) en lied 9 ..."; "... woordmelodie; doch waar er in het volgende vers op dezelfde muziek een ...". Brandel 1961 on it: "In the Babira language, for example, a word like kókó (chicken) which has a high, even pitch in a sentence is usually placed high in a song; a descending word like kapè (visible) generally has descending musical tones ... hî ga (hearth) gets two descending tones on the first syllable. See W. P. Maeyens ... Kongo-Overzee, IV (1938), pp. 250-259." [English of the Dutch: 'a word with a level high or low word-melody keeps this property in (song) ... tone of the first stem syllable. See song 5: hîgă (hearth) and song 9'; 'word-melody; but where in the following verse on the same music a ...']
sources.locator: Google Books search-only snippets of Kongo-Overzee 4 (1938), p. 250 ff.; Brandel 1961 The Music of Central Africa (Nijhoff; Springer reprint 2012 id 5EGSBgAAQBAJ), footnote citing Maeyens pp. 250-259
sources.note: Early first-hand note explicitly about 'musical accent with semantic function' (i.e. tone vs. accent) in Bira; would settle whether prominence is tonal and may comment on dynamic stress.
